The pair is excluded because the memo counts only pairs strictly below the line

answer.exemplar: The objective 3b + 4r is linear, so its greatest value over a bounded region must occur at a corner point. List the corners of the feasible region, evaluate 3b + 4r at each one, and pick the largest result. Checking only one corner is not safe, because a different corner can give a larger value even when the chosen one looks balanced, and the corner where two boundary lines cross is not always the winner.

questions.explanation: A linear objective is extreme at a corner, so list the corners, evaluate 3b + 4r at each, and take the largest. Reading one corner only is not enough, since another corner may score higher.
questions.hint: A linear objective is best at a corner, so check them all.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Vertical boundary line and the side it shades
questions.learningObjective: describe a vertical boundary and the side a rule shades
questions.stem: A markets memo lists corridor lengths: east | 1500 feet, west | 2200 feet. The memo sets the rule x >= 1500 for the east corridor and asks which side is shaded. Explain what the boundary line looks like and which side of it the rule shades.

answer.exemplar: Because x appears on its own, the rule x >= 1500 has a vertical boundary line at x = 1500, running straight up and down the graph. The inequality shades the side to the right of that line, since values of x of 1500 or more lie there, and the line itself is included. Every point to the left of x = 1500 fails the rule, no matter what its y value is.

questions.explanation: A rule with only x and a constant gives a vertical boundary, and the sign of the rule picks the side. Here x >= 1500 shades everything to the right of the line at x = 1500, including the line.
questions.hint: Picture the graph with x on the horizontal axis.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Points exactly on a boundary line

questions.stem: A harbour memo lists block measures: park | 5 units, retail | 7 units. The memo allows 3p + 5r <= 60, and the planner claims the pair (4, 9) lies exactly on the boundary. What is the actual value of 3p + 5r at that pair?
questions.explanation: Substituting p = 4 and r = 9 gives 3(4) + 5(9) = 12 + 45 = 57, under 60. The pair sits strictly inside the region, not on the boundary, where the value would be exactly 60.
questions.hint: Substitute the pair and compare the result with 60.

options.text: The corner is (60, 0), and the objective 5p + 4o there equals 300
The corner is (0, 40), and the objective 5p + 4o there equals 160
options.misconception: picks the corner on the vertical axis instead

options.text: The corner is (30, 20), and the objective 5p + 4o there equals 230
options.misconception: picks a point on the line that is not an axis intercept

options.text: The corner is (60, 0), and the objective 5p + 4o there equals 120
options.misconception: reads the constant in the rule as the objective value

questions.explanation: The line 2p + 3o = 120 meets the horizontal axis where o = 0, giving p = 60. At that corner the objective 5p + 4o is 5(60) + 0 = 300, so the constant 120 in the rule is not the answer.
questions.hint: Set the other variable to 0 to find the axis intercept.

Which corner gives the greatest value of 5c + 8r?

options.text: The corner (100, 120), where 5c + 8r equals 1460
The corner (0, 180), where 5c + 8r equals 1440

options.text: The corner (280, 0), where 5c + 8r equals 1400
options.misconception: picks the cleanup corner without comparing the values

options.misconception: assumes the smallest corner must give the best value

questions.stem: A dwellings memo lists land uses: housing | 2 units, office | 4 units. The rules are 2h + 4o <= 400, h + o <= 150, and the memo also says both values are at least 0. A planner ignores that last condition and reports the region as unbounded. What is the error?

options.text: With both values at least 0 the region is a closed polygon, so a rule that closes it was dropped
The region really is unbounded, because a rule on a sum cannot bound two values
options.misconception: believes a sum rule cannot bound a region

options.text: The non-negative rule has no effect, since any real value can be increased
options.misconception: thinks non-negativity never changes a region

options.text: The polygon would have only three corners, so the planner report is right in spirit
options.misconception: invents a corner count for the wrong region

questions.explanation: With h and o at least 0 the rules cut out a closed polygon with corners (0, 0), (150, 0), (100, 50) and (0, 100). Dropping the non-negative rule is what made the region look open.
questions.hint: Check which rule the planner left out of the picture.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Unbounded feasible region
questions.learningObjective: explain why an objective can have no greatest value
questions.stem: A theatre memo lists permit types: tree | 100 dollars, sign | 150 dollars. The memo allows any number of tree permits but no more than 3 sign permits, and it never caps the total dollars. Explain why no greatest value of 4t + 9s can be found for this plan.

answer.exemplar: The rules are t at least 0 with no upper limit and s at most 3, so a plan may include 1, 2, 3 or 100 tree permits, and nothing forbids more. Since 4t grows by 4 for every extra tree permit, the objective 4t + 9s can be made larger at any time by adding another tree permit, so the set of objective values has no greatest member. Only a rule that caps every direction of the region can produce a maximum.

questions.explanation: The tree count has no cap, so adding a tree permit always raises 4t + 9s. An objective that can always be improved has no greatest value, which is what the missing cap causes.
questions.hint: Ask whether one more unit could always be added.

questions.explanation: The total rule allows at most 50 workers and the night rule needs at least 10, so the smallest night crew is 10. That leaves 50 - 10 = 40 day workers, the most that still meets the minimum.
questions.hint: Use the smallest night crew the memo allows.

options.misconception: includes a pair that exceeds the zoning limit

The pair lies on the boundary, but the planner used the rule 2p + 3r >= 50

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Objective value read at a corner point
questions.learningObjective: explain why every corner must be checked for the best objective value
questions.stem: A towers memo lists options: bus | 2000 dollars, bike | 800 dollars. The rules are 2b + 3k <= 600 and b + k <= 200 with both values at least 0, and the objective is 5b + 2k. Explain how a planner finds the corner with the greatest objective value and why checking one corner is not enough.

answer.exemplar: A corner of a bounded region is a point where two boundary lines meet or where a boundary line meets an axis, so the planner first lists the corners of the feasible region. Then the objective 5b + 2k is evaluated at each corner, and the largest result is the answer. One corner is not enough because the objective is linear in two variables, so a different corner can produce a larger value even when the first one looks balanced.

questions.explanation: List the corners of the region, evaluate 5b + 2k at each, and take the largest. One corner is not enough, because a linear objective can be larger at a corner that looks less balanced.
questions.hint: The objective is linear, so compare all the corners.

An unbounded region, because the two lines meet at only one point

At least 3 more means w <= p + 3, so the direction of the sign does not matter

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Counting whole-number points in a region

questions.stem: A depot memo lists lane lengths: short | 3 blocks, long | 5 blocks. The memo allows at most 20 blocks of new lane and at least 1 of each type. Explain how to count the whole-number pairs of short and long lanes that fit.

answer.exemplar: The rule is 3s + 5l <= 20 with s and l whole numbers of at least 1, so fix l first and count the s values that still fit. With l = 1, the short lanes may run from 1 to 5; with l = 2, from 1 to 3; with l = 3, from 1 to 1; and with l = 4 the 20 blocks are already used, leaving no room. That gives 5 + 3 + 1 = 9 whole-number pairs.

questions.explanation: Fix the long count and count the short counts that still fit: 5, 3 and 1 for long counts of 1, 2 and 3. A long count of 4 already uses all 20 blocks, so there are 9 pairs.
questions.hint: Start each count at 1 and work along the rows.

questions.topic: Non-negative constraints in a counting model
questions.learningObjective: describe how non-negative rules shape the counting work
questions.stem: A boulevards memo prices two request types: street | 300 dollars, sidewalk | 500 dollars. The memo allows 300x + 500y <= 2400 and counts only whole requests of at least 0. Explain how the rule that both counts are at least 0 shapes the counting work.

answer.exemplar: The non-negative rules cap the search: because x and y cannot be negative, only the first quadrant needs to be examined, and the money rule then bounds each count from above. For a sidewalk count y of 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 the street counts that fit run from 0 up to 8, 6, 4, 3 and 1, and a fifth sidewalk request would need more than the whole budget. The work is therefore a short list of columns rather than an endless plane, and every pair counted is a pair of real request counts.

questions.explanation: Because both counts are at least 0, only the first quadrant is examined and the budget then bounds each count from above. The work becomes a short list of columns of real request pairs.
questions.hint: Ask how the region changes when negatives are ruled out.

questions.stem: A estates memo lists work orders: trees | 3 units, signs | 5 units. The rules are 3t + 5s <= 60 and t + s <= 18 with both values at least 0. What is the value of t at the corner where the two boundary lines cross?
questions.explanation: The corner satisfies 3t + 5s = 60 and t + s = 18, so t = 18 - s. Substituting gives 3(18 - s) + 5s = 60, which simplifies to 2s = 6 and s = 3, so t = 15.
questions.hint: Solve the second rule for t, then substitute it in.

questions.stem: A gardens memo lists project types: planting | 2 units, hedge | 1 unit. The rules are p >= 0, t >= 0 and t <= 3, and the objective is 5p + 2t. First state whether the region is bounded, then state what happens to the objective as p grows.

The region is unbounded, and the objective 5p + 2t stays at its largest value

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Vertical boundary line and the side it shades
questions.learningObjective: describe how a vertical boundary shapes a region with a second rule
questions.stem: A boardwalks memo lists corridor widths: east | 900 feet, west | 1400 feet. The memo sets the rule x >= 900 for the east corridor and also requires x + y <= 2000. Explain how the vertical boundary in the first rule shapes the shaded region once the second rule is added.

answer.exemplar: The rule x >= 900 draws a vertical line at x = 900 and shades everything to its right, so the region has no points with an x value under 900. When the rule x + y <= 2000 is added, the region is cut by a second slanted line, and the shaded area becomes the part of the half-plane to the right of x = 900 that also lies under that line. The vertical edge stays a straight line running up and down the graph, while the other edge is slanted.

questions.explanation: The vertical rule shades everything to the right of x = 900, and the second rule cuts that half-plane with a slanted line. The region is the overlap, with one vertical and one slanted edge.
questions.hint: Picture the two shaded half-planes and their overlap.
